title: Wallcovering Fire Ratings: British Standards and Commercial Specification
description: How reaction-to-fire classes such as B-s1,d0 are read, which standards and guidance apply in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and what makers' documents show for specific commercial wallcoverings.
cardDescription: What B-s1,d0 and Class 0 mean, England's Table 6.1 and the other UK nations, and what named makers' documents show for specific commercial wallcoverings.
metaDescription: Wallcovering fire ratings explained: Euroclass decoder, BS EN 13501-1, Approved Document B Table 6.1, Class 0 history, and product evidence from named makers.

scope.jurisdiction: England first (Approved Document B), with Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland set out separately. Not legal advice for any other country.
scope.review: Sources are rechecked each quarter and whenever a regulator or maker publishes a change. Each product row carries its own checking date.
scope.notice: General specification guidance, not project-specific fire-safety approval. The classification a wall or ceiling needs, and whether a proposed installed build-up achieves it, must be confirmed by the responsible project professional: the designer, fire engineer or building-control body.

decoderIntro: A European reaction-to-fire class has up to three parts: the main class (A1 to F), a smoke subclass (s1 to s3) and a flaming droplets subclass (d0 to d2). Read the notation exactly as the document prints it. If a subclass is not printed, it is unknown, not assumed.
sourcesIntro: Every document cited on this page, grouped by where it comes from. For standards we link the publisher's catalogue record, which confirms the title and edition; we have not reproduced paid standards. For manufacturers we link their own published documents rather than copying them. The checking date is when we last opened each source.
cta: Send the product references, the rooms or areas they are for, and the fire requirement each area carries, if you know it. We will tell you which documents the maker publishes for that product, what build-up they describe, and the questions to put to the maker and the project's fire specialist before anything is ordered.

checklists.title: Before ordering
checklists.intro: Collect these for each wallcovering and each area it is going into.
items: The exact product: maker, collection, product reference, colourway or design, and whether it is a stock or digitally printed version.
The construction as supplied: face material, backing, weight and any finish or protective coating.
The requirement for each area: the class the project's fire strategy, designer or building-control body has set, and whether the area is a room, a small room or a circulation space.
The evidence: the current declaration of performance and, where available, the classification report for that product, with their references and dates.
The tested build-up: the substrate, adhesive and any primer or lining named in the classification document, and the field of application it allows.
The proposed build-up on site: the actual wall, any existing finishes, the lining, primer and adhesive to be used, and any coating to be added.
Any difference between the two, with the maker's written clarification and the project professional's acceptance.
The maker's installation instructions for that product, current at the time of ordering.

checklists.title: At handover
checklists.intro: Keep a record of what was actually installed, so it can be checked later.
items: A room-by-room or area-by-area schedule of the products installed: reference, colourway and batch number.
Copies of the declaration of performance, classification evidence and installation instructions relied on, with their dates.
The adhesive, primer and lining actually used, with batch numbers where practical, and the substrate each area was hung on.
Any approved variation from the documented build-up, with the maker's clarification and who accepted it.
Photographs of the prepared substrate before hanging, where the project calls for them.
Care and cleaning instructions, including any limit on later coatings or overpainting that would change the build-up.
Spare material from the same batch, labelled, for future repairs.

faq.q: What does B-s1,d0 mean on a wallcovering?
faq.a: It is a European reaction-to-fire classification under BS EN 13501-1: class B for the main fire behaviour, s1 for the lowest smoke production category and d0 for no flaming droplets or particles in the test. It applies to the product as tested, in the build-up the classification document describes.

faq.q: Is B-s2,d0 good enough for a hotel corridor?
faq.a: That depends on the requirement set for that corridor. In England, Approved Document B's Table 6.1 guidance gives a minimum for circulation spaces that B-s2,d0 can meet, but a project's fire strategy can set a higher requirement, and the product must be installed in the build-up its classification covers. The designer, fire engineer or building-control body decides.

faq.q: A data sheet says only 'Euroclass B'. Is that the same as B-s1,d0?
faq.a: No. 'Euroclass B' without smoke and droplet subclasses tells you the main class only. Treat the subclasses as unknown and ask the maker for the declaration of performance or classification report, which will state them.

faq.q: Is Class 0 the same as a Euroclass?
faq.a: No. Class 0 is an old British national classification defined in Approved Document B by reference to BS 476 Part 6 and Part 7 results. There is no automatic conversion between Class 0 and a European class. England's guidance stopped offering national reaction-to-fire classes as an alternative from 2 March 2025, subject to transitional arrangements.

faq.q: Does a fire-rated wallcovering make a wall fire resistant?
faq.a: No. A wallcovering's class describes its reaction to fire: how it contributes to the early growth of a fire. Fire resistance, expressed in minutes, belongs to walls, floors and doors as building elements, and a wallcovering does not provide it.

faq.q: Can a classified wallcovering be hung over old wallpaper or lining paper?
faq.a: Only if the maker's documents or written confirmation say so. Hanging over an existing wallcovering adds an untested layer, and makers' instructions generally require old wallcoverings to be removed. Lining paper, a different adhesive or a later coating are also changes to the build-up.

faq.q: Does Mr Wallcover certify the fire rating of what it installs?
faq.a: No. Classification comes from testing and classification of the product in a stated build-up, and the manufacturer declares the performance. We install the specified product to the maker's instructions and record what was installed. The responsible project professional accepts the evidence.

faq.q: Do these rules apply in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?
faq.a: Each has its own building regulations and guidance: Approved Document B in Wales, the Technical Handbooks in Scotland and Technical Booklet E in Northern Ireland. They use the same European classes but their tables, terms and amendment dates differ, so check the guidance for where the building is.
